heading: Induction behaviour recurs across model families, sizes, training runs and modalities
definition: heads with induction behaviour appear across model families, sizes and training runs (and in other architectures or modalities).
summary: Several independent groups reproduce induction behaviour across model families, sizes and training runs, and some report it in other architectures and modalities. How much induction behaviour causally contributes to performance varies with the model and test.

suggested_status.by_scale: Toy: R2 for tested synthetic induction settings (arXiv:2609.19000#R14, arXiv:2609.19000#R23, arXiv:2609.19000#R24). <1B: R2 for occurrence across tested text transformers (arXiv:2605.24059#R1, arXiv:2605.24059#R10, arXiv:2605.24059#R14), with a stated scope limit, not C, for functional induction in Pythia-160M under the conditions of arXiv:2605.08853#r1 and arXiv:2605.08853#r3; other groups report Pythia-160M induction heads with ablation effects (arXiv:2605.24059#R10, arXiv:2608.22007#A1-P160-5h). 1–10B: R2 (arXiv:2605.24059#R18, arXiv:2605.24059#R19, arXiv:2505.18752#r16). 10–100B: R2 for induction-scored heads with classification-ablation effects in Llama2-13B/70B and Llama3-70B (arXiv:2505.18752#r13, arXiv:2505.18752#r01, arXiv:2505.18752#r07). >100B: ?; counts: versions.V4.studies_by_size has no '>100B' entry.
suggested_status.reason: Groups other than the original's report induction-selective heads and causal copying effects across GPT-2, Pythia and OLMo (arXiv:2605.24059#R1, arXiv:2605.24059#R10, arXiv:2605.24059#R18, arXiv:2605.24059#R19), supporting R2 for occurrence in tested settings. The weaker OLMoE matched-random differential concerns causal specificity, not head absence (arXiv:2605.24059#R22). Pythia-70M retains induction behaviour after its score declines, also supporting occurrence (arXiv:2609.19000#R7). The Pythia-160M functional-absence result is recorded as a scope limit, not C. The scale defines C as a failed replication or a credible artifact argument, and the rules define no condition-specific C. In that result, Pythia-160M has ICL advantage −7.668 and no meaningful damage through 20 greedy head ablations on 200 random repeated-token sequences (arXiv:2605.08853#r1, arXiv:2605.08853#r3). It comes from one preprint whose header gives controls n, uncertainty n and code n. No induction-specific matched-random controls are reported, and the checkpoint identifier is not stated. The verdict for this condition is limits_scope; the checked against item labels it challenges. That study's Figure 6 shows a dominant layer-8 induction-attention cell, so functional absence cannot establish absence of induction-pattern attention. On the same model, other groups report causal effects. Ablating two heads lowers synthetic induction top-1 from 4.7% to 0.05% at the final checkpoint (arXiv:2605.24059#R10). Mean-ablating five heads picked by induction-offset attention destroys 60.0% of clean induction gain; no five-head Pythia control is reported (arXiv:2608.22007#A1-P160-5h). A prefix-matching induction head also forms early in Pythia-160M training (arXiv:2601.21996#R4, figure-only; a score, not a causal test). None of these four studies shares authors with an original. Counts: versions.V4.tested_with_controls = 46 and versions.V4.tested_with_code = 33 describe the supplied records. The verdict aggregates predate the checker's label corrections and require regeneration; no corrected totals are inferred.
suggested_status.open_questions: Apply a common induction criterion, specified checkpoints, matched prompts and controlled ablations to resolve the Pythia-160M functional disagreement (arXiv:2605.08853#r1, arXiv:2605.08853#r3; arXiv:2605.24059#R10). A replication of Pythia-160M functional absence at a stated checkpoint, with induction-specific matched-random controls and uncertainty, would make C a candidate again. So could a rule from Iris that a condition-specific challenge gives C, applied to all seven versions, or her reading of arXiv:2605.08853 alongside arXiv:2605.24059. Tests above 100B would establish a currently uncovered scale (counts: versions.V4.studies_by_size). Independent replications in other architectures and modalities, and direct head measurements across large-model training runs, would determine how far the text-transformer R2 assessment extends.

source.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads

original_result.setup: The original study measured induction-head prefix matching, a score for attending to continuations of earlier matching patterns, during training in 34 decoder-only Transformer language models from four model series.
original_result.result: Induction heads formed abruptly, but did not form in one-layer models. A 13-billion-parameter model contained heads for literal copying, translation and pattern matching, with respective prefix-matching scores of 0.75, 0.85 and 0.94, where higher scores indicate stronger attention to continuations of earlier matching patterns.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: OPT-66B contains plausible induction heads in its upper layers.
Induction heads develop across all four seeds of a small attention-only transformer.
GELU-2L and GPT-2 Small contain heads with induction behaviour.
Induction heads emerge at similar training stages across most tested Pythia sizes.
A 162M Llama model develops induction heads during training.
GPT-2 Small fine-tuned for word-level tokenization shows induction attention on repeated natural text.
Without positional encodings, a transformer copies induction-style when training is less repetitive and prefixes are long.
Induction circuits recur across five initialization seeds of the same small model.
Induction heads are examined across 12 models spanning several language model families.
A six-layer NanoGPT model qualitatively shows induction-head retrieval.
Disrupting the induction path severely impairs forward copying across Llama, Qwen and GPT-2.
Mamba-130M implements an induction circuit through its state-space mechanism.
GPT-NeoX develops heads attending to tokens after earlier matches across seeds and model sizes.
GPT-2 and all three tested Pythia sizes transition to attending to tokens after earlier matches.
Induction-like attention patterns recur across toy embedding variants and five seeds.
Every evaluated decoder model contains heads scoring highly on repeated-token induction.
Induction heads emerge across 35 GPT-2 and Pythia models.
In-context learning appears, then fades, across seeds; initialization shifts when this happens.
Heads attending to tokens after earlier matches enable nonsense-token copying in Llama-2, Llama-3 and OLMo-2.
Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B contain heads scoring highly for attending to tokens after earlier matches.
Induction behaviour appears even when a transformer's query and key weights are held fixed.
Fresh training runs using a Pythia-style setup develop induction heads at two model sizes.
Induction-score peaks span tested sizes and training-data schedules, with weaker peaks at 1B parameters.
Exact image repetitions elicit a head attending to immediately preceding tokens and induction-style retrieval.
Induction-ranked heads matter more than random heads across tested Llama and Gemma models.
All 12 tested Pythia, GPT-2 and Llama 2 models contain high-scoring induction heads.
Head ablation destroys in-context prediction in tested Pythia and Qwen2.5 models.
Induction or copying emerges across Pythia and OLMo families and multiple seed configurations.
Text and multimodal Qwen models share induction heads and heads attending to immediately preceding tokens.
Ablating heads selected using repetition lowers predicted enhancer (gene-regulating DNA) activity in both Evo 2 sizes.
GPT-2, Pythia and Llama share circuits with induction heads and heads attending to immediately preceding tokens.
Llama 3 and GPT-2 architectures learn induction circuits across tested depths on Gaussian Match-and-Copy.
Induction heads appear across toy-model seeds, a LLaMA-style model and OLMo-1B.
Disentangled and standard transformers learn the same induction circuit: copy, then match.
Two bidirectional protein language models contain distinct groups of induction heads that causally affect behaviour.
Induction appears in autoregressive and diffusion models, including forward and reverse diffusion runs.
Induction heads form across four Pythia sizes from 14M to 160M.
All baseline retraining seeds develop induction heads alongside previous-token heads.
A transformer using multi-head latent attention, which compresses keys and values, develops five induction-pattern heads.
Induction circuits precede induction behaviour across tested combinations of Pythia or OLMo models and tasks.
Induction heads help recall next items in known sequences in tested Qwen2.5, Gemma and Mistral variants.
Spatial cellular-automaton transformers develop induction-style circuits across designs and settings.
Small head sets mediate synthetic induction across GPT-2, Pythia, OLMo and OLMoE.
Chronos contains cross-attention heads meeting criteria for copying and attending to tokens after earlier matches.
Successor-value heads recur across all three seeds of a soft-prior transformer.
Pythia binding and transport effects recur across independent runs and probe domains.
GPT-2 Small exhibits induction behaviour, with related heads reported in GPT-2 Medium.
Induction heads appear with hyper-connection residual variants (mHC, mHC-lite) and standard residual connections.
SpiritLM contains heads attending to tokens after earlier matches for both speech and text.
Hybrid models share transformers' induction circuits: previous-token information plus finding matching tokens across the sequence.
Induction-head ablation reduces recall of next items in known sequences across Llama, Mistral, Qwen and Gemma.
Heads selected for induction account for substantial copying improvements in GPT-2 Small and Pythia.
Pythia, OLMo and OLMoE each develop several heads highly selective for induction.
Repetitive training or short prefix matches favour positional attention over content matching.
Mamba implements induction through convolution and recurrent state rather than attention heads.
Pythia-6.9b shows less separation between token and concept induction roles.
Clustered image-label sequences without exact copies yield image-label mapping without heads attending to immediately preceding tokens.
Pythia-160M lacks functional induction under the tested prediction and ablation measures.
Pythia-70m induction scores decline late in training.
Induction circuit patterns are less clear with RoPE and ALiBi.
Peaks in recalling next sequence items and their attribution to induction heads vary across base models.
OLMoE induction-head ablation has only a modest advantage over matched random ablation.
Pure Gated DeltaNet (GDN) retrieves through recurrent state, with little transfer from earlier source positions.
Targeted induction-head ablation has weak or absent effects at some Qwen and Gemma settings.

untested.what: Non-attention architectures beyond Mamba-130M (one size, one run) and GDN hybrids: RWKV is examined only for SAE feature similarity, not induction. Also natural-image vision transformers and encoder-only text models. Modalities tested are protein, DNA, time series, speech, Omniglot image-label and cellular automata.

wording_issues.issue: In Mamba-130M the induction circuit runs through a local convolution plus SSM state, not heads, and writes one token late (B1+1 −9.69 vs B1 −0.0 at distance 8). A pure GDN without global attention has historical-source Carrying <0.02 (vs 2.60 with full attention) and retrieves via recurrent state. 'Heads' only fits these architectures as an analogous circuit (verdict on 2410.06672).

What counts as 'induction behaviour' differs by study: prefix matching ≥0.3 (Llama-3-8B ~3% of heads; Chronos 8.3% of 144 with copy ≥2 SD), top-10% ranking (2505.18752, which always returns heads, per verdict), and ≥50× selectivity (2606.02378). In 2607.23054 the scores are 0.194–0.250 with no threshold or baseline stated. Many verdicts note that attention-pattern scores do not test copying or composition with a previous-token head.

Functional induction and induction-pattern attention require separate readings. On random repeated-token sequences, Pythia-160M has ICL advantage −7.668 and no meaningful ablation damage, challenging functional induction in that condition; its layer-8 induction-attention cell prevents inferring absence of induction-pattern attention. In 2509.22947, final-checkpoint induction signatures occur at 0.13B, 0.5B and 1B in one decoder-only architecture. Peak scores are near 1.0 at 0.13B/0.5B and well below 0.5 at 1B: this establishes a strength difference, not nonuniform presence. In 2511.16893, model size is a non-significant predictor of emergence across GPT2/Pythia configurations.

Run-to-run evidence is mostly toy-model seeds. Induction heads appear in every seed but at different head indices: 1:6/1:7 vs 1:1/1:3 in 2410.02984, and a different head per seed in 2609.10287. The original reports one training run per model. So 'appear across training runs' holds for presence, not for which heads.

The Omniglot comparison uses GPT-2-style models with MLPs: previous-token heads form with exact instance copies but are absent in the compared bursty sequences without exact copies. In a transformer with MLPs and no position encodings, α≥1 gives content preference with ≥3-token prefix matches; α=0.1 prefers position even at the longest window. These averaged attention preferences do not establish induction-head absence; all tested models retain some content sensitivity. In a multimodal two-layer decoder, RoPE produces a more diffuse correct-label induction peak than APE, while the peak persists. These results distinguish data-dependent circuit formation from differences in attention preference or circuit strength.

method_sensitivity.what: Which heads count, and how many, changes the ablation outcome. Pythia 1B synthetic induction top-1 (baseline 4.05%) goes to 0.25% with 3 heads at ≥50×, 0.05% with 6 heads at ≥30×, and 0% with 11 heads at ≥10×. Pythia 410M (baseline 3.7%) goes to 0.10% with 8 heads at ≥100× and 0.0% with 11 heads at ≥50×. Chronos's 8.3% count is threshold-sensitive, and top-10% ranking always yields heads.

method_sensitivity.factor: Number of ablated heads and random-head controls
method_sensitivity.what: In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, the targeted change grows with head count: −2.62e-6 (1 head), 1.57e-5 (10), 7.45e-5 (50), 7.93e-5 (100). Random 50/100-head ablations also cut 2.49e-5 and 3.17e-5. Heads needed for 80% damage: 2 in Qwen2.5-0.5B (GQA), 22 in Pythia-1.4B and 28 in Pythia-6.9B (MHA). In DCLM-trained OLMoE 1B-7B's final checkpoint, induction-circuit ablation reduces synthetic induction top-1 by 4.80 percentage points versus 3.50 for matched-random heads, a reported 1.4× differential. This weaker specificity concerns causal attribution, without establishing absent induction heads.

method_sensitivity.factor: Prefix length of the repeated sequence
method_sensitivity.what: arXiv:2406.17759 reports GPT-2 Small head 5.1's induction attention rising from <0.3 to >0.7 with prefix length. Corrupting long-prefix examples to one-prefix examples reduces its average induction score from 0.55 to 0.05, effectively stopping induction. That paper reports head 5.5 starting at 0.7 for short prefixes and retaining 0.43 after corruption. lw:xmegeW5mqiBsvoaim supports the qualitative prefix dependence and the approximately 0.55→0.05 corruption result, but gives an approximately 0.45 comparator with a repeated H5.1 identifier, leaving its head attribution ambiguous. The numeric prefix-length endpoints are attributed to arXiv:2406.17759.

In arXiv:2601.20796's multimodal two-layer synthetic decoder, RoPE gives more diffuse previous-token and induction patterns than APE; the correct-label induction peak persists. In arXiv:2607.06621's pretrained RoPE models, zeroing the RoPE phase of previous-token heads raises induction-task cross-entropy 0.52→2.24 (Pythia-410m), 0.56→1.11 (Pythia-1.4B) and 0.30→0.91 (Llama-3-8B).

Mistral-7B-v0.1 base peaks at lag 0 (copying, S3), while Mistral-7B-Instruct shows a lag +1 peak. For the instruct checkpoint, Table A3 reports lag +1 probability of 0.04366 under random 1-head ablation and 0.06869 under random 100-head ablation (S22); it supplies no zero-head row. The variants differ in aggregate temporal output patterns; these differences do not establish absence of induction-behaving heads. For base Mistral, 100-head induction ablation changes lag +1 probability 0.00060→0.00012; random 100-head ablation gives 0.00085 and shifts the peak from lag 0 to lag +1 (S10, S18).

arXiv:2407.10949 reports data-dependent attention preferences: at α = 0.1, averaged final-layer attention prefers position even at the longest matching-prefix window; at α ≥ 1, it prefers content with at least three matching tokens. All models retain some content sensitivity; these comparisons do not establish induction-head absence. In arXiv:2501.06256's compared 3-layer, 1-head GPT-2 models with MLPs on Omniglot, previous-token heads are absent under bursty training without exact instance copies and form with exact copies (r1, r2). Copy curricula shift the induction-peak depth by about 2–3 layers relative to the natural-only baseline (2509.22947 R02, R06, figure-only).

method_sensitivity.factor: Patching position and layer in non-attention architectures
method_sensitivity.what: In Mamba-130M, patching the SSM input at B1+1 drops B's logit by −9.69 and −11.25 (distances 8, 16). At B1 the effect is −0.0 to −0.01 at every distance. The layer-17 state gives −8.09 to −10.16. Where one patches decides whether the circuit is seen.

method_sensitivity.factor: Prompt set and metric in instruct-model ablation comparisons
method_sensitivity.what: On random-token serial recall, arXiv:2510.22752 reports targeted +1-probability reductions for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct of 9.35e-5 (1 head) and 2.24e-4 (100). Gemma-2-9b-it gives −6.59e-6, −1.31e-5, 1.72e-5 and 1.53e-5 at 1, 10, 50 and 100 heads; random 100-head ablation gives 7.27e-6. arXiv:2604.01094 uses 500 frequent English words with 5000 permutations: after 100 targeted ablations, absolute lag +1 probability is 0.00060 for Llama and 0.00157 for Gemma. Random-ablation probabilities increase from 1 to 100 heads: Llama 0.00066→0.00167; Gemma 0.00496→0.01436. Table A3 has no zero-head row. These studies differ in ablation sensitivity and causal specificity under different prompts and reported metrics.

In arXiv:2604.01094's base checkpoints, using repeated shuffled lists of 500 frequent English words with 5000 permutations, Llama-3.1-8B has weak lag +1 preference: probability is 0.00103 unablated, 0.00092 after 100 induction-head ablations and 0.00934 after 100 random-head ablations. Gemma-2-9b gives 0.07125, 0.00206 and 0.00478 respectively, so random ablation also strongly reduces successor retrieval. The study reports stronger lag +1 reductions from zero ablation across all layers than from mean or half-layer ablation. These output and control effects concern intervention specificity; they do not establish absence of induction-behaving heads.

In public Pythia-70m checkpoints, the per-head prefix-matching induction score falls from a peak of 0.93 to 0.36 at 67B tokens; induction behaviour remains present. In arXiv:2501.06256's 3-layer, 1-head GPT-2 with MLPs on Omniglot, trained with burstiness and exact instance copies, initially high layer-2 image-label retrieval attention declines alongside ICL. These results describe changes over training; the Pythia decline does not limit V4's appearance claim.

status_amendment.public_note: The suggested rating for this version changed from contested back to independently reproduced. One preprint found no working induction circuit in a small Pythia model, but other groups find induction heads with causal effects in that same model, so the result is now listed as a limit on scope.
status_amendment.level_changed_because: C to R2. The C rested on one condition-specific result (arXiv:2605.08853#r1, arXiv:2605.08853#r3) from a single preprint. Its header gives controls n, uncertainty n and code n, and no induction-specific matched-random controls are reported. Its checkpoint is not stated, and its own Figure 6 shows a dominant layer-8 induction-attention cell. The verdict model labelled it limits_scope; the checked synthesis relabelled it challenges. The project scale defines C as a failed replication or a credible artifact argument and has no condition-specific C. On the same model, other groups whose headers report controls and code find induction heads with ablation effects (arXiv:2605.24059#R10; arXiv:2608.22007#A1-P160-5h, for which no five-head Pythia control is reported). A prefix-matching induction head also forms during training (arXiv:2601.21996#R4). Occurrence is independently reproduced across families and sizes, so under the rules as written R2 with a stated Pythia-160M scope limit fits. Iris's pending cross-version rule, or her reading of arXiv:2605.08853 against arXiv:2605.24059, could restore C.
